author: kevinmcconnell
body:
What purpose is `Bubble::Thread` serving? It feels to me like the bubble owns the comments & system messages that make up its conversation thread. So it can own that association directly.

Maybe we can simplify this a little to:

- A `Bubble` `has_many :messages`
- A `Message` is a delegated type. The `Messageable` types we have are `Comment` and `EventSummary`.
- An `EventSummary` `has_many :events`.

This maps onto the same mechanism you already have here, which is that:

- Certain actions in the system generate events
- When a new `Event` is created, we also add it to the appropriate `EventSummary` (creating it if necessary). That way the system messages are built out at save time, and rendering them is cheap (and cacheable).

I'm not 100% sure of the naming here: there's probably a better word for `EventSummary`, and `Messageable` doesn't exactly roll off the tongue. But it'd be something like that.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
> an explicit AR thread model (which seems odd but gives us an idiomatic cache expiry mechanism and more natural language)

Re the caching of the `Thread` model, do you mean you wanted an additional level of fragment caching between the `Bubble` and it's `Threadable`s? I'm curious whether that would matter in practice, since a lot of `Bubble` changes will presumably also be adding events. I'd guess it's more important that each `Threadable` gets cached. But in any case, we could separate that fragment out without giving it its own model if it's worthwhile?

In terms of language, I think "a bubble has many comments" feels more natural than "a bubble has one thread, which has many comments". But maybe I'm missing something here! Did you find some parts come out more awkwardly without that model?

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
Yes, the naming might be the only thing suggesting it! "Thread entry" is a tricky name because of that, it implies there is a "Thread" they belong to, whereas having a collection of "Comments" didn't imply any sort of "Comment list". But aside from the names, the relationships are equivalent. I reckon the "thread entry" name is just a little misleading.

I almost wondered if the `Entry`/`Entryable` naming, like in HEY, could work here. It doesn't feel quite right to say "a bubble has many entries", but it's close. On the other hand, we're showing two types of message on the bubble: user messages (comments) and system messages (event summaries), which is what led me to think of this as `Message`/`Messageable`. Something along these lines could make sense.

author: josefarias
body:
One thing about having a materialized `thread` is that we can also later have a concept of a global `timeline`, and we can choose to relay events to the `thread` and/or `timeline` as needed. That's what the rollup kind of is — a relay mechanism. But that's getting too far ahead of ourselves.

Let's go with the simplest architecture for now (likely your proposed `Message/Messageable` directly on the bubble, which doesn't impede relaying to a timeline either) and accept that this is in flux so we can keep iterating on everything. I'm not sure we know enough about the product yet to make a definitive decision here. As long as it's easy to change, cache, and paginate (which we do know we want) we can move forward.

I added a few thoughts on first read through. But the main thing I'm wondering is, do we need to save a view for every bucket (and have buckets associated with views like this), or can we simplify views to just be filtering conditions?

Conceptually I'd been thinking of the current view as the set of filters currently applied to `Bubbles#index` via the query string. When browsing the bubbles you can change the filters around however you like, to control what's shown there: different tags, different buckets, assignments, etc.

If you want to save one of those, you're effectively persisting that query string, so we need a per-user model to put that in, along with a name if you want to name it, etc. But built-in views (like a view per bucket) don't need to be saved, because they haven't been customized. So I don't think those need to involve the view model.

What do you think?

Similarly, you can change the filtering options that you're looking at without saving anything; it's only if you want to explicitly save one for later that you have to create a view model I think?

I think this is fine, so this is just me wondering out loud but...

Rather than build a query string ourselves, we could use a form with `method="get"`. The nice part about that is it's leaning on the built-in browser behaviour; it's just how the Web works, and it doesn't need JavaScript to do it. It's also agnostic to the fact that Turbo is involved. And we wouldn't need to merge anything if the existing state is in the form already.

The downside is the form would submit all the empty params as well, so the query strings would be longer and uglier. We could use a Stimulus controller or a Turbo hook to strip the empty fields out prior to submit, but that might end up cancelling out the benefits from not building the query string manually :)

So quite possibly it's not worth it, but I thought it was an interesting alternative to consider just in case.

It _was_ that! I got it working like this:

```rb
def persist!(attrs)
  create_or_find_by!(creator: attrs.delete(:creator), params_digest: digest_params(attrs)) do |filter|
    filter.assign_attributes attrs
  end.tap(&:touch)
end
```

I think the current version is nicer though:

```rb
def persist!(attrs)
  create!(attrs)
rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
  find_by!(params_digest: digest_params(attrs)).tap(&:touch)
end
```

I'm thinking to keep us moving I'll go with the latter for now.

We considered this sort of design as well:

```rb
class Message < AR
  after_create :captured
  after_destroy :uncaptured

  private
    def captured
      messageable.captured_as(self)
    end

    def uncaptured
      messageable.uncaptured_as(self)
    end
end

class Comment < AR
  def captured_as(message)
    message.bubble.comment_captured
  end

  def uncaptured_as(message)
    message.bubble.comment_uncaptured
  end
end
```

But it felt premature in that comments are the only kind of messageable (of which there's _only_ two now) that needs to notify the bubble it's been captured.

We can migrate to that design if needed. Doing _the simplest thing_ for now.

author: josefarias
body:
I thought about introducing this at this level:

```rb
has_many :accesses, dependent: :delete_all do
  def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
    return if proxy_association.owner.all_access?

    transaction do
      grant_to granted
      revoke_from revoked
    end
  end
  # ...
end
```

But that only introduces the guard when revising. Which is fine, but misleading. The crux of being _all_access_ isn't that you're unable to revise access. It's that you're unable to remove access (by illegitimate methods, since the UI won't allow this). Granting access is a non-issue because it's granted automatically — and you can't remove it.

Don't have super strong feelings either way, but this feels like the right level to perform the check.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
Came here today to say something similar. I was thinking about this PR last night, and it occurred to me that all of the more complex parts (and all of the issues raised on the PR) are really about the non-tenanted side of things. And that side really only exists as an abstraction for renaming databases, which is something we haven't fully explored yet. Having non-tenanted models and non-tenanted states at all is YAGNI at this point.

The original design was that a multi-tenant version of the app was exactly like the single-tenant version, except that it connected to the slug-determined DB at the start of each request/job. The beauty of that is the simplicity. It's really a single, tiny change to the architecture. I think we should try going back to that design, and completely ditch the non-tenanted models.

We can treat updating a slug as its own feature later, and if we find we need some shared state to do that safely we can introduce it then. But we might not need it!

I also don't even know that we need to hash the slug to create the DB name. Slugs will already have restrictions on chars/length/etc, so they could equally be filesystem-safe. I don't think this matters much

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
One other thing I was thinking about though, with regards to renaming, is that we should maybe be using the shard names on directories rather than files. Since SQLite DBs are actually a group of 3 files (.db, .db-wal, .db-shm) which all share the same base name, it might turn out simpler if instead of

    /storage/production/{shard}.db
                       /{shard}.db-wal
                       /{shard}.db-shm

we could do this:

    /storage/production/{shard}/main.db
                               /main.db-wal
                               /main.db-shm

That way renaming a database is a single, atomic filesystem operation.

There's still some racey parts to consider but I bet we could work around those.

I think, as discussed previously, it's probably still worth splitting the House rendering work to its own branch while you explore that. Unless you're confident that it's definitely the right approach. But I think what I'd be trying to answer there is: what limitations are there in a hand-built Markdown renderer, compared to something like Redcarpet?

My hunch is that there are a bunch of edge cases to consider with Markdown rendering, especially with things like formatting that's inside other formatting, and so on. House is able to render some reasonable subset of Markdown in order to provide format previews while you're editing. But it's OK if it doesn't support everything. You can still put in any Markdown text you want, and even if it's not something House knows how to deal with it'll still work -- it just might not get previewed. But, once you actually save some markdown content, you'd want that to render accurately.

But I haven't looked closely at this, so maybe that's a bad assumption on my part! I'd be interested to hear what you find out about it.

I did the work to get rid of this "fake shard" and ran into the propeller that is Rails's lazy loading of model attributes from the database.

Concrete example: the "first run" view calls `User.new` to build the form, which will try query the database the first time an attribute check is done. But we're not connected to a tenant database and can't resolve the attributes:

```
/home/flavorjones/Work/basecamp/active_record-tenanted/lib/active_record/tenanted.rb:46:in `connection_pool'
rails (5520bd835e37) activerecord/lib/active_record/connection_handling.rb:310:in `with_connection'
rails (5520bd835e37) activerecord/lib/active_record/attributes.rb:243:in `_default_attributes'
rails (5520bd835e37) activemodel/lib/active_model/attribute_registration.rb:38:in `attribute_types'
rails (5520bd835e37) activerecord/lib/active_record/attribute_methods.rb:260:in `_has_attribute?'
rails (5520bd835e37) activerecord/lib/active_record/inheritance.rb:61:in `new'
app/views/first_runs/show.html.erb:13
```

I'm going to fall back to a "fake shard" implementation for now, but I'll be careful not to expose it to the app. Let me know if you have other ideas on how to resolve this.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
This is a great start!

I've left a few comments/thoughts. In the main, I think we should try to split this a bit differently. With this PR, a Markdown attachment is specifically associated with a `Bubble`, and it happens that we only use `has_markdown` on `Comment` which is also owned by `Bubble` (indirectly), so that works but it feels quite tied to that structure, and could complicate things if we want to add another markdown field anywhere else.

What if instead we tried it like this:
- Markdown attachments are associated with whatever record owns the markdown. In our case, that'd be `Comment`.
- `has_markdown :body` defines a `body` association (as it does now), but also defines a `body_attachments`
- For convenience, we'd probably define a `has_many :comment_attachments, through: :comments` sort of thing (in our case there's actually a delegated type in the middle of this too, but that should be fine)

That feels like a cleaner separation to me. It's also one step closer to an extractable Action Text integration that we can eventually upstream.

What do you think?

author: kevinmcconnell

Adding a file into the markdown field of an object seems like it's creating an attachment for that object. Maybe "upload" is not even a concept we need here.

This raises an interesting question! If this comes up, I assume it's because content was pasted from one bubble to another. But that seems like it should be allowed, and it's probably useful to do it sometimes. And even if it hasn't happened yet, presumably it could in the future?

Then if we're relying on the association for things like showing related attachments for a bubble, or GC-ing attachments after a bubble is edited/deleted, the results might not be what we expected.

Maybe this is spilling over into another topic, but could be worth thinking through to make sure we've got this right. Can attachments belong to multiple bubbles? Or should linking to an existing attachment duplicate its reference somehow? Or am I misunderstanding it and this isn't actually a problem? :thinking:

author: kevinmcconnell

I think we should try to keep any app-specific models out of the action_text portion here. Partly for future attempts to extract this, but also in case we want to stick a markdown area on some other model in the app. Like, maybe we want to let you add a bio to your profile, and write that in markdown; or add a description section to a collection, or whatever.

Maybe we should associate the attachments with the `record` that the markdown field is on. We can still get them from the bubble with a `has_many :comment_attachments, through: :comments` sort of thing. But it would let the attachment/markdown logic stay agnostic to what sort of models it's being used on.

I don't _think_ we'll currently hit that problem because of the way we autosave everything -- the record will exist by the time you can add an attachment to it. author: jorgemanrubia
body:
There was an issue rendering tons of cards and, for each card, rendering all the turbo-frame powered popover bits (e.g., tags, people, etc.). This would trigger a ton of concurrent requests when rendering the list, which I strongly suspect is the culprit for the performance issues in staging. In production, we have this problem, too, but we don't render as many cards. Also, the more powerful servers could mask the issue, absorbing all the requests.

I went with a helper to set a preview context when rendering the cards. I think this was better than the alternatives:

- Create completely separated templates for preview and regular view/edit, just to exclude the turbo frames. Since these are complex templates with subpartials, that would result in a messy setup if we tried to reuse the common bits, which is essentially everything except the turbo frames.
- Passing down some sort of "editable" param, which would propagate through a ton of templates used in many different scenarios.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
I like that this structure matches how we track `popped` cards -- the presence of the record gives it a state.

But, that said, I started to wonder if, now that we have this 3-column state, should we actually move this to an enum? Now that we're getting into the presence/absence of multiple associated records, to determine something that is really a 3-way switch, it is a little more complicated. So maybe a card could have three positions it could be in, which are 3 enum states: `considering`, `doing` and `completed`.

That would also guard against the state where a card accidentally ended up being both `considering` and `popped` or whatever. Because I think with the current modelling this can happen:

```
b = Bubble.find(...)
b.engage
b.pop!

b.popped? # true
b.doing? # true
```

We could alternatively make those actions more aware of each other, so that engaging removes the pop and so on. But as I say, feels like it's getting a little more complicated.

The downside to a single state is that the `Pop` is currently letting us track the user & timestamp of the completion, so we'd need to track those elsewhere. But maybe worth considering.

What do you think?

body:
@jorgemanrubia I think the approach makes sense, but I also had a different idea in mind and wondered what you think of this as an alternative. The way I see it, mentions are not themselves notifiable things, because they always happen in the context of some other event that _is_ notifiable: a new comment, a new card, etc. So I think the mentions state is more a property of the resource, and instead of adding new notifications we just need to make the current notification content reflect that.

For example, if I create a comment that mentions you, I don't think you need to receive both of these:

- "Kevin commented on {card}"
- "Kevin mentioned you on {card}"

I think the second implies the first, and can be thought of as just the "commented" notification being a bit more detailed. (cc @jzimdars -- does this sound right to you?).

We do something similar(ish) already with assignments: we don't send you a "Kevin created {card}" if we're already sending you "Kevin assigned you to {card}".

So what I had in mind is that we could keep notifications on events, because everything that's notifiable is a trackable event, by design. And instead the flow works something like this:

I still think it's a good idea to enforce basic security at the domain model level. E.g: that's what we do in BC4 `Subscribable`: when you add subscribers, you make sure they are reachable in the bucket. If we place this responsibilty in the caller, someone adding auto-watching in the future may forget and leave an exploit to add unauthorized watchers open. It's the kind of things hackers target, don't you think?

author: jorgemanrubia
body:
I understand why you took this approach, but I feel that "local time controller" is generic in nature, and this change is coupling it with cards and bubbles quite a bit. As you point out, generating such an amount of markup in the stimulus controller feels a bit off.

Instead, I'd consider creating a controller for these bubbles. It could be something like "card bubble controller". I'd try to keep it not tied to "closing" as we should be able to use the same for the "reconsider" scenario as per this https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/pull/497#issuecomment-2881589715.

We could keep the markup in the ERB, 

```erb
<% if card.auto_close_at %>
  <%= tag.div class: "card__bubble", data: { controller: "card-bubble", card_bubble_date_value: card.auto_close_at.to_i } do %>
    <svg viewBox="0 0 200 100">
...
```

And you could use stimulus targets for the different parts of the bubble: e.g: text, unit, value

```erb
<textPath href="#top-half" startOffset="50%" dominant-baseline="middle" data-card-bubble-date-value-target="text">...
```

I'm not sure if we would need to hide these depending on the value specifically, but that's something the controller could do if needed.

An alternative to this approach is to load the extension via the database.yml file:

```yml
production:
  primary:
    <<: *default
    database: storage/tenants/<%= Rails.env %>/%{tenant}/db/main.sqlite3
    tenanted: true
    extensions:
      - ./bin/lib/beamer.so
      - <%= SqliteVec.loadable_path %> # this line would replace this file
```

Additional benefit, then this extension isn't loaded into cache/cable/queue databases.

author: flavorjones
body:
Just FYI: I looked into this, and this is probably fine.

The sqlite-vec extension creates several tables behind the scenes, including (but probably not limited to):

- search_embeddings_chunks
- search_embeddings_info
- search_embeddings_metadatachunks00
- search_embeddings_metadatachunks01
- search_embeddings_metadatatext00
- search_embeddings_rowids
- search_embeddings_vector_chunks00

However, since they're created at runtime by the extension, this _shouldn't_ be a problem for us when migrating.

Note for future us: if we ever remove sqlite-vec, we should remember to delete these tables as well as `search_embeddings`.

author: flavorjones
body:
The HTML5 spec provides a simpler definition for email addresses than RFC 5322, intended for input field validation but probably perfectly fine for this purpose:

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#email-state-(type=email)

and it even provides a regex for its definition:

```
/^[a-zA-Z0-9.!#$%&'*+\/=?^_`{|}~-]+@[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?(?:\.[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?)*$/
```

which looks the same as the one used by `URI::Mailto::EMAIL_REGEXP`. We could probably just replace the start and end anchors with `\b` and use that, if you wanted something a bit more robust.

But, to be honest, what you have is probably perfectly fine, too.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
We should consider adding a short public cache expiry to the public views, something like:

```ruby
expires_in 5.seconds, public: true
```

It's short enough that the views will stay current, but means that if you get a burst of traffic most of it can be handled by the intermediate proxies/CDNs (Thruster, Cloudflare, etc).

That way if someone shares a public link that gets a ton of traffic, the Rails app is protected since it only needs to do one request every few seconds to keep up.

author: jorgemanrubia
body:
The index should include `card_id` as the first column so that you can quickly query the steps for a given card:

```ruby
add_index :steps, %i[ card_id completed ]
```

Think of an index as an additional table where you can query by the columns it includes quickly. If you want to query "give me the steps for the card with id 123", you need that column to appear in the index, or the DB will have to scan through all the rows in the table to locate the steps for that card.

author: jorgemanrubia
body:
It's great to have a gem to centralize this logic! For your consideration: I think it would be fine if the gem just exposed the API to unfurl the link (e.g: to get the title for the link), and then the host app introduces its own controller using that gem. That would simplify the authentication stuff and, more importantly, would allow different apps to configure the unfurl logic differently. This goes in the line of the suggestion about whether Lexical should support getting arbitrary HTML replacements for links.

For example, In Fizzy, we could choose to present "Fizzy links" with some custom HTML, while in Basecamp, we present those as regular links. Or we could choose to unfurl other types of links differently (E.g: PDF links using the PDF viewer in Basecamp). Both apps could use the same API to extract the title of "supported apps links", but would assume how to present the links (even if we duplicate the same rendering logic in both apps, I think that's fine).

> I considered using regular Rails caching, but it seemed too weak. The summaries we generate are meaningful pieces of information. I think it makes sense to make them a first-class citizen.

I agree, I think this is spot on 👍

There's another reason I wanted to mention for doing it this way too: with our replicated SQLite setup, each app server will have its own cache (because we can't share those databases across servers, and we want the cache operations to be local and fast). This means that cache content will get duplicated, which in most cases should be fine (it's just a few more cache misses), but in this case we wouldn't want to have to regenerate the content on each server. But storing the content in the model solves this, because it will replicated along with the rest of the app data.

author: jorgemanrubia
body:
The `limit` param results in having to pass it down the pipeline to several other methods. Methods like `cost(within:)` or `cost_microcents(within:)` read a bit awkward. The shared param is often a smell that something is missing.

Also, all the methods here are public. Only `limit_cost` and `cost` should be public, right?

Thinking about how to clarify this, my mind goes to having a new record `Ai::Quota` so that each user has a quota. The quota has an amount that gets reset weekly in a cron job (it can have an anchor date `reset_at` to fetch the accounts to reset). Whenever you incur AI expenses, you subtract from the quota (if not exceeded).

This way you remove the responsibility of tracking AI quotas and raising quota errors from the conversation. The quota record is the place to implement the limit. 

Also, this way you don't depend on messages being removed or not, and you don't have to sum them. Whenever you create a new message, you can track the quota in the user.quota record (maybe in a callback?).

author: jorgemanrubia
body:
I'll coment more on this below, I don't feel these accessors are entirely justified.

If you wanted to make an AR attribute, you can use a custom Active Model/Record type; there is first-class support for it. You can define a type, register it, and then declare attributes with it. The type will take care of casting on assignments and also on serialization logic when dealing with the DB. Essentially, here you could do:

```ruby
attribute :used, :money_type
attribute :limit, :money_type
```

As a bonus this would work with active record queries too! E.g: `.where(money: "100$")`, not that we need that here.

You can see `AllDayDateType` in HEY too (although the declaration there is a bit more complex because there is conditional logic).

This is from ChatGPT:

```ruby
class JsonHashType < ActiveModel::Type::Value
  def cast(value)
    case value
    when String
      JSON.parse(value) rescue {}
    when Hash
      value
    else
      {}
    end
  end

  def serialize(value)
    value.to_json
  end
end

# config/initializers/types.rb
ActiveModel::Type.register(:json_hash, JsonHashType)

class MyModel < ApplicationRecord
  attribute :metadata, :json

author: monorkin
body:
Oh, I forgot about the attribute API.
Thank you for the explanation and examples!

I'll bunch together a few answers to your comments surrounding the custom type:

I went with the custom type because it makes it easier to use and reason about the limit and usage attributes.

My concern is that `quota.limit # => 2000000000` isn't understandable at a glance, while `quota.limit # => Money` and then `quota.limit.in_dollars # => 20.0` is.

The money type provides fixed-point arithmetic backed by an INTEGER.
SQLite allows you to define a column as `DECIMAL(10,8)`, which would remove the need for fixed-point conversion.
But, after reading the [docs](https://www.sqlite.org/datatype3.html#affinity_name_examples), I learned that SQLite treats DECIMAL as a NUMERIC which is in term backed by a double precision float.

Floats have various odd behaviors that cause them to produce errors over time, which I wanted to avoid
```
sqlite> SELECT (0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1) - 0.3 as difference;
5.55111512312578e-17
```

I might be too pedantic here.
Using a NUMERIC might be good enough, and the small errors will likely amount to peanuts given that we'll reset them weekly.
What do you think?

author: jorgemanrubia
body:
On the what's public side, I'd use the rule of not adding public methods that are not used anywhere. The narrower the public surface of a class the better, since it's easier to grasp its responsibilities at a glance. If you saw a public `reset` method, you may wonder where the decision of resetting a quota is made. The fact that it's private, instantly signals that the reset logic is handled internally. So what's public and private matter a lot. I just wouldn't add public unused methods. If the method is used internally, make it private. If, in the future, someone needs to invoke it, then make it public. 

> Is there someplace I can read up on what drives the decision to extract something into a concern vs inlining the methods in the main object? Or is there a rule of thumb I can use?

We don't have that documented. We normally use concerns for auxiliary traits of a class. If we make the whole reset behavior private, as so far it's handled internally, I think it makes sense in the main class. The main class exposes a couple of public methods. Those methods use the reset methods internally. Since those are internal, I think the private section is a better fit that a separate con

body:
I don't know really! Mostly just wondering out loud.

Two things we could perhaps consider are:
- Never invalidate a webhook on a successful response. Only do the check on failure. That way if it just took someone a while to get things set up right on their end, they wouldn't see a success followed by invalidation.
- To handle the lower-volume ones, what if we set the limit to something like "all requests failed for the last 10 requests, or 4 hours, whichever is longer". That way even something that only fires twice a day will still invalidate eventually if it keeps failing. But for something that's firing a lot, it doesn't get invalidated simply due to something brief like a server restart or transient routing problem. It we track total failure count and first failure time (and reset them both to nil on success), then it should be simple to check.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
I think the logic here is sound, but to me (and this is quite subjective), the concept of high volume vs low volume makes it a bit less clear. It makes it sound like there's two different categories of webhook depending on traffic. Also resetting only happens for "high volume webhooks", which makes me have to think about why low volume webhooks don't.

I think it'd be simpler to structure this more like:

- You track consecutive failures as they occur. Whenever a delivery succeeds, those stats get reset.
- On failure, check whether the webhook now meets the conditions for "delinquent". To be delinquent you need to have tracked x failures for at least y minutes.

I think this boils down to the same thing, but to me it feels more obvious and has fewer concepts: no more high/low volume, or resets being due or not due, etc.

The reason it helps, I think, is that it clearly separates the act of tracking from the act of checking for delinquency. Those are two separate steps. Whereas with reseting based on volume, it's sort of mixing the two.

Does that make sense?

Nice, I think that turned out to be clear & simple in the end! :raised_hands: 

Minor thing, `enough_time_passed?` would be a clearer name if it explained "enough time for what?". Feels like it's missing just a bit of the its meaning there.

I can't think of a great name right away, but maybe more along the lines of `failing_for_too_long?`. Perhaps you could extract both parts of the checks so that each gets a name and the main condition ends up being something like `failing_for_too_long? && too_many_consecutive_failures?`. I think there's probably a better way to say it, but _something_ like that :)

Or even just inline them both so you get:

```ruby
first_failure_at&.before?(CHECK_INTERVAL.ago) && consecutive_failures_count >= DELINQUENCY_THRESHOLD
```

Could even name those constants more similarly (because `CHECK_INTERVAL` implies it's how often you check for delinquency, but actually you check on every send. It's more like the duration it has to stay broken for). So maybe name them like:

```ruby
first_failure_at&.before?(DELINQUENCY_DURATION.ago) && consecutive_failures_count >= DELINQUENCY_THRESHOLD
```

That's a very minor comment though. It looks good as-

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
Reading back what I just wrote there, I think there's something to the idea of getting a method like:

```ruby
def delinquent?
  failing_for_too_long? && too_many_consecutive_failures?
end
```

Because as a reader trying to understand that delinquency logic you're going to naturally find that method, and then that one line basically summarises the logic that it uses. (I still suspect you could improve on the precise naming of it, but I like the idea of the method :)).

One question I have -- and I think this is currently in-flux anyway with the discussion of linking accounts with different email addresses -- is whether we can/should move the creation of the new tenant to _after_ the magic link step.

I think that would help because:
- We get email address validation before creating a new database. While that's not perfect, it goes a long way to avoid malicious or accidental requests flooding us with a bunch of new tenant DBs. It means you at least need to go through that dance once before you can create a database; and once you're authenticated we could also limit how many/quickly you could create any subsequent ones.
- I think we could then have "Create account" be an option on the same magic link landing page. We could style it differently depending on whether you had existing accounts (but still might want to add another one), or this was your first.
- If you create a new one we can link it then bounce you to the tenanted path to create and populate the DB (possibly moving the actual creation into a job while the front end waits for it to complete, as we discussed).
- All of this would be linked by a single email address still.

author: flavorjones
body:
I'm going to push back on this note a tiny bit harder. Looking into it, the code that would need to change to support a `published_at` timestamp:

- a view helper that would choose `created_at` for draft cards and `published_at` for published cards
- complicating the `Card.chronologically` scope to use `created_at` for draft cards and `published_at` for published cards
- changing Filter to use `created_at` for draft cards and `published_at` for published cards

And you very well might say, "But we don't display draft cards anywhere, so we don't need to switch which date we use based on card status! Just always use `published_at`.", but this seems like an implicit admission that we don't really care about the `created_at` value, which is kind of my point.

My mental model is that a draft card is a very ephemeral thing. A card becomes concrete at the moment of publishing -- that's its essential moment of creation -- and tracking the timestamp of when the draft was created feels very unnecessary to me. And the code above from BC3 (which was introduced in 2016!) seems to support that mental model.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
An alternative to sleeping the request (and wasting Puma worker time) would be to lean on the reproxy feature we built into Kamal Proxy. With that we'd end the request with a header that asks the proxy to present the same request again after a short delay. (Sleeping in the proxy is very cheap because it has massive concurrency.) We could also use that to shunt the request over to the primary if the replica still hasn't caught up after a bit, but that brings the obvious risk that increased replication lag could lead to overloading the primary and become a cascading failure.

In practice I think it'll depend on how much, and how often, we expect to see lag. If it's rare and short, a sleep might be just fine as a way to paper over the occasionally stale read. If it's more common we'll need something more robust; but if it's much more common then writer pinning was probably the better answer in the first place anyway.

Yes, I think a middleware makes most sense. The concern is just an easy place to test things out first.

More generally, the part I was wondering about is whether we should lean on the proxy layer to help with this. If we don't, it's nice that this could be self-contained: we could allow configuring the poll interval and max delay, but otherwise all you'd need to do is enable the middleware and it works. But the downside would be if we had a sustained period of high replica lag, suddenly all the requests that follow a recent write become slower, which could affect capacity. Which would be implemented as 

```ruby
def without(*symbols, &block) 
  niled = symbols.map { [ it, nil ] }.to_h
  with(**niled, &block)
end
```

<details>
 <summary>Demo Script</summary>


```ruby
class Something
  attr_accessor :a, :b, :c

    @a = 1
    @b = 2
    @c = 3
  end

  def to_s
    "@a=#{@a}, @b=#{@b}, @c=#{@c}"
  end

  def without(*symbols, &block)
    niled = symbols.map { [ it, nil ] }.to_h
    with(**niled, &block)
  end
end


s = Something.new
puts "Before 'without': #{s}"

s.without(:a, :c) do
  puts "Inside 'without': #{s}"
end

puts "After 'without': #{s}"

author: djmb
body:
I think there are some interleavings here that can give errors if the table is initially empty. If two requests both don't find the record they'll then try to create it. 

I think the unique index on value will ensure the second one to create a record will fail, but it's kind of an inelegant way to enforce that. Making the value unique doesn't really express what we are trying to do here and the second attempt failing relies on the fact that they both try with the same initial value.

Maybe a separate field that has a unique index where we always use the same value would be a better fit. And using `create_or_find_by!` to ensure that the second concurrent request finds the row the first request created if it's own create fails.

Something like this on the table:
```
  t.string :lock_key, default: "singleton", null: false
  t.index :lock_key, unique: true
  t.remove_index :value
```

And then:
```
  def with_lock
    transaction do
      yield lock.create_or_find_by!(lock_key: "singleton") do |sequence|
        sequence.value = initial_value
      end       
    end
  end
```

body:
I wonder if this could be simplified using the built in [authenticate_or_request_with_http_token](https://api.rubyonrails.org/v7.1/classes/ActionController/HttpAuthentication/Token.html). 


something like 

```ruby 
def authenticate_by_bearer_token
  authenticate_or_request_with_http_token do |token, _options|
    access_token = Identity::AccessToken.find_by(token: token)

    if access_token&.allows?(request.method)
      Current.identity = access_token.identity
    else
      # Returning false from the block makes Rails send 401
      false
    end
  end
end
```

author: umarhadi
body:
Two changes will make this config clearer and more reliable across providers:

1. Rename `aws` to `s3`
   The current name implies vendor-specific behavior, but this config works with any S3-compatible service (R2, MinIO, Tigris, DO Spaces). Using `s3` reflects the protocol, not the vendor.

2. Add checksum configuration for non-AWS providers
   [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/#checksum-types) and some MinIO setups reject the default `CRC64NVME` checksum and return `InvalidRequest: You can only specify one non-default checksum at a time`.

   Suggested config:

   ```ruby
   s3:
     service: S3
     # ...existing config...
     request_checksum_calculation: <%= ENV.fetch("S3_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION", "when_supported") %>
     response_checksum_validation: <%= ENV.fetch("S3_CHECKSUM_VALIDATION", "when_supported") %>
    ```

    For R2/MinIO users:
    ```bash
    S3_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=when_required
    S3_CHECKSUM_VALIDATION=when_required
    ```

This keeps AWS behavior unchanged while ensuring compatibility with other S3 providers.

author: jorgemanrubia
body: Ideally, we would enqueue the job in an `after_commit` callback. However, the fact that an Action Text record touches the record itself breaks our traditional pattern of remembering data via instance variables across callbacks (the instance itself can change). A potencial problem here is if the callback triggers the delta update but then the commit fails to run for whatever reason. That would result in the wrong delta accounted for. Since these are very rare, I think it is fine to just accept the small variations those could produce (in exchange for keeping the code simple).

author: packagethief
body:
Here I think we'd just iterate over the cards and ask them to recalculate themselves, taking care of their own dependents.

Each class that includes `::StorageTracking` is responsible for providing `recalculate_bytes_used` and having it return the new value. They can implement their own caching policy as they see fit. Cards and comments, for example, don't cache the value, but having them do so would be easy to add.

```ruby
# Account::StorageTracking
def recalculate_bytes_used
  boards.find_each(&:recalculate_bytes_used).sum.tap do |value|
    update_column :bytes_used, value
  end
end

# Board::StorageTracking
def recalculate_bytes_used
  cards.find_each(&:recalculate_bytes_used).sum.tap do |value|
    update_column :bytes_used, value
  end
end

# Card::StorageTracking (doesn't cache the result)
def recalculate_bytes_used
  bytes_used = rich_text_associations.sum { # ... }
  bytes_used + comments.find_each(&:recalculate_bytes_used).sum
end
```

If we need to in the future, we could implement a more efficient `calculate_bytes_used`. It would use cached values where possible without performing a full recalculation.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
This looks great @harisadam, thanks for getting it started. I've left a few suggestions, all minor things though!

I also think we might want to flip this around so that the env is `MULTI_TENANT`, and by default the app runs as single tenant. I _think_ that is actually the behavior that people self-hosting the app are mostly likely to want. Because if you're running the app for yourself, you probably don't want to let random strangers come along and sign up for accounts on your server :) So `MULTI_TENANT` seems like it should be opt-in. Having the default this way means one less ENV for people to think about in the common case.

If we do that, we will also need to be able to have our fizzy-saas gem opt in to `MULTI_TENANT` as well. We could use a config value for that (similar to what's [happening here](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/main/config/initializers/content_security_policy.rb#L7-L8)).

> narrow definition of Open Source being the definitive word on "open source"

@dhh To touch briefly on the aside, the case to be made for having a "narrow definition" is that it enables other systems to be built on top of it. Is the 8-bit byte a "narrow definition"? Sure, but without it we wouldn't have modern digital computing. Abstractions involve tradeoffs, and the case for a narrow definition of "open source" is that the tradeoff enables further systems to be built atop it, such as legislation. The CRA/PLD would be way worse without a carve-out for "open source software stewards," and that carve-out can't happen without a clear definition.

author: ezekg
body:
I agree with you, i.r.t. the OSI not having a monopoly on the term "open source." They don't, and I'm not a fan of the people who police the term either. But I also think clear communication matters more than any one term or definition matters, and right now, using the term "open source" communicates the free gift to some, but it miscommunicates to others.

And [miscommunication is bad communication](https://37signals.com/30), right?

I think "fair source" could be a way to communicate the gift of Fizzy, but also the user freedoms, the limitations, and even more, the company's goal i.r.t. sustainability, while championing open source and the spirit of open source. You could argue the license text does just that, which I'd agree with -- but the term "open source" does not. I think there's a way to communicate things in a way that doesn't cause the endless drama loop that surrounds the words "open" and "source" in close proximity.

I think fair source communicates these things clearly, and most importantly, *honestly.*

Perhaps this is a battle you want to take, and kudos to you if so. I do believe there's value in something new, though, and without baggage. 37signals would b

author: dhh
body:
I appreciate you trying something new here. I think there are room for many license experiments. I, for example, consider the obligation under the GPL to contribute back all changes to be a far more onerous limitation on open source than "you can't run a competing SaaS". But there's room for disagreements here too.

Which is part of why I just don't buy into OSI's narrow definition. Open source describes perfectly well what's happening right now with Fizzy. The code is there, you can run it yourself, you can make changes, if you'd like to share those, we'll review them as PRs, and we'll include them as future releases. The entire life cycle of open source as understood by people without an ideological allegiance to OSI's framing know what this is.

Then the particular restrictions, whether that's on the SaaS carve-out or the obligation to contribute back any changes, are spelled out in the license. As it ever was.

Anyway, we're not interested in relinquishing the SaaS rights to Fizzy on any set timeline, so a fair software license isn't for us. But love that you guys are giving that angle a go and that it works with your objectives ✌️

author: jankeesvw
body:
When importing GitHub issues to Fizzy, the `created_at` is correctly set from the original GitHub with this PR. However, `last_active_at` is always set to the import timestamp ([via this `before_create` callback](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/5d181af3912424074a5166147c33ba37a02def6e/app/models/card/eventable.rb#L7)).

This causes two issues:

1. **Sorting is incorrect** - Cards in the triage column are sorted by [`last_active_at`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/5d181af3912424074a5166147c33ba37a02def6e/app/models/card.rb#L24), so all imported cards have the same "last activity" (the import time) instead of their actual last activity on GitHub. This can be fixed by carefully importing in the correct order (but is not great).

2. **"Not now" does not work properly** - Automatic postponing of inactive cards is based on `last_active_at`. Since all cards appear as if they were "active today", old inactive issues do not get automatically moved to "Not now".

@jeremy What do you think would be the best approach to fix this? 

One option would be to make `last_active_at` settable via the API (like `created_at`), and change the `before_create` callback to `self.las

author: elalemanyo
body:
Thanks for the feedback @jorgemanrubia!

Totally understand that devcontainers aren’t part of your current workflow. The intention behind this PR isn’t to change how the project is developed or require anyone to use devcontainers, but to provide an **optional** setup for contributors who want it.

Rails offers devcontainer support as an option, and many people in the Rails community use it to get an application running quickly without having to install or align local dependencies. For open source projects especially, this can lower the barrier to entry for first-time contributors: clone the repo, open it in a compatible editor, and the app is ready to run.

This setup doesn’t affect existing workflows, CI, or production in any way—it’s purely additive. If someone doesn’t use devcontainers, they can simply ignore the files.

From my perspective, this is mainly about improving onboarding and making the project more accessible to the wider Rails community. Of course, I’m happy to adjust or remove it if you feel it doesn’t align with the project’s goals.

Thanks for considering it! 🙂

I'd say that's true for PWAs, too. I know accessibility experts and tools all hate when you do this but the user experience of being able to pinch/zoom inside of an app isn't great and breaks the illusion of native in our hybrid apps.

> @dilberryhoundog that seems unrelated to this PR. I'll take a look at your PR in a bit.

@monorkin  Thank you. Yes it was unrelated. 
Although the hotkeys have now been disabled in the not_now column the bug on 6e90a6dbf commit was:

---

# Bug: Card duplication when closing from Not Now

## Root Cause

When closing a card from "Not Now" using the `]` hotkey, the Turbo Stream response failed to remove the card from its source location. The `capture_card_location` method only tracked `@source_column` (nil for postponed cards) and `@was_in_stream` (false for postponed cards), leaving no condition to handle the Not Now case. This caused the card to appear in both Done and Not Now until the next page refresh.

## Fix

```diff
--- a/app/controllers/concerns/card_scoped.rb
+++ b/app/controllers/concerns/card_scoped.rb
@@ -21,6 +21,7 @@ module CardScoped
     def capture_card_location
       @source_column = @card.column
       @was_in_stream = @card.awaiting_triage?
+      @was_postponed = @card.postponed?
     end
```

```diff
--- a/app/views/cards/closures/create.turbo_stream.erb
+++ b/app/views/cards/closures/create.turbo_stream.erb
@@ -4,6 +4,8 @@

Also a minor thing, but something about having this clause here seems a little complicated to me. I think it's because it's covering two different types of situation in the same method. We're checking:
- Is the account active?
- Does the current identity have a user in the account?

Those are two different situations, but their details are mixed. And this method is only called by the `before_action` when `account.present?` as well, so the details are also a bit split, into two places.

Maybe worth extracting a method for each of those, so that the logic in the action is more obvious? Something like `account_active?` and `user_active?` maybe? And that could also cover the conditional that's attached to the `before_action` so we could simplify that.

It's not a big deal either way, but it just seems like it's starting to get intertwined a bit.

While working on this I also came up with a completely different approach for doing the OSS <> SAAS integration using callbacks.

They look like the perfect use-case for this.
The OSS part just defines the callback points, and the SAAS gem adds whatever callbacks it wants.

To me this seems more readable than the placeholder methods used in other parts of the app, and nicer than having a dummy subscription object (given that the fake subscription object is implemented through a active_subscription method that would get complicated, and the need for some kind of FakeSubscription in the OSS version)

Curious as to what you think of this approach.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
Yes, I really like this way! I think for the immediate case we could've gotten awary with simply adding a method to `Account` that we override in the concern. But using callbacks makes for a nicer separation, and also means people could hook in other custom behavior to those events for their own integrations.

Could even consider defining helpers to make these look more like AR callbacks, along the lines of:

```ruby
def self.after_cancel(...)
  set_callback :cancel, :after, ...
end
```

...so that the billing integration can then just say

```ruby
after_cancel -> { subscription&.pause }
```

But up to you if you think that's worth it. In any case, I think the callback approach is a good call :+1:

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
Yes, I think that helps!

Actually looking at it now, it's probably fine to inline those two methods if you want, because the rest of the changes simplified it enough that they read better. Now that it boils down to just `unless Current.account.active? && Current.user&.active` it's actually quite clear. The other changes (negating the conditional, safe navigation operator, named action condition etc) have made it less of a mouthful than it was before :) Either way though, this looks clear to me now.

author: nqst
body: Thanks @andyra! I love the idea, but I think we still need to use the magic number. The default panel paddings are quite generous, so if we just subtract the current panel padding from its radius, we'll have an inner radius of 0. I experimented a bit and ended up with this: ```css --panel-inner-border-radius: max(calc(var(--panel-border-radius) - var(--panel-padding)), 0.5em); ``` This way, the radius never gets too small. If the parent panel radius is larger, it works as expected: But since that's not the case, I'm not sure if it's worth making it more complex. I didn't open a PR, but you can see the working code here: https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/compare/main...nqst:fizzy:inner-panel-dynamic-radius

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
I quite like the structure of having the `RecordSet` types, but I notice that most of them are very similar. The bulk of them boil down to "get all the records by account ID, store into a path based on the name". Which, I think, is what we were originally hoping the whole import/export process could be.

I realise that as we get deeper into it, some of the models might deviate from that a bit. But maybe we could try to really push back on the number of deviations where possible, and then have hooks for anywhere we do need to handle something in a different way. That way the bulk of the process could use the same pattern without having to restart parts of it on each model.

So if the places where it strays from convention are few and minor, do you think we could push some of this up into the base class, and then all the "normal" tables could avoid needing to implement most of the methods here?

Or, alternatively, could we avoid deriving individual classes at all, expect in the cases where a table has some special behaviour? So if a model needs a special join, or some pre/post processing we can specify just those parts?

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
If we did try to collapse the record set classes a bit, we could handle this in a sort of `before_insert` step so that we don't need to supply a full implementation of `import_batch` to do it.

I also wonder if the export half of this is necessary (converting sgids to gids) or could we implicitly trust the signing on the way in while converting to new sgids? Effectively re-signing from an unknown key to the valid one. Since the transfer is effectively trusting that aspect of the input data anyway, it could be one less step. (Not sure if it makes much difference in practice or not though.)

author: kevinmcconnell

Hey @andyra, it looks like there are two separate but related changes in here:

1. `Card.mentioning` selects `status: published`
2. `Search::Record.search` joins against the `cards` table to select `status: published`

I'll write separately about each.

I don't think this change is necessary! Although `Card.mentioning` by itself will return cards in "draft" status, it's only called in two places.

The first call site is in `app/controllers/prompts/cards_controller.rb` (used for Lexxy card autocompletion), where it's added to a query that is already filtering for published cards:

    def search_cards

        .mentioning(params[:filter], user: Current.user)
        .reverse_chronologically
        .limit(MAX_RESULTS)
    end

    def published_cards
      Current.user.accessible_cards.published
    end
```

author: adjogima
body:
We use some custom components and the `env()` values reported by the system are not right on all sides.
`safe-area-inset-bottom` will account for the app switcher handle at the bottom but not the tab bar.
So we can't default to env()

The apps measure and inject the right value(s) at runtime.

The reason I made both a `--injected` and `--custom` version of the variables is to make sure the apps can inject a custom inset when needed but we'd still give it a chance to fall back to `env()` before assuming `0px`. And it happens in CSS land, the apps can't mess it up, they just add `--injected` variables, the web side decides what to do whit it.

author: monorkin
body:
Tested the migration on staging. 
Backfilling card_id took 15min, while creating the stacks took 30min.

I could speed this significantly up by moving the migration into SQL, but that would require me to write one query for MySQL and another for SQLite.

The better tradeoff here is to split the migration into a schema change, and a data migration, then deploy the schema change first, run the data migration from the console, and then deploy the data migration to clean up any stranglers.

author: kevinmcconnell
body:
I'm "lightly nervous" about using models in the migrations in this case. For our SaaS environment, we know that migrations will be short-lived and safe. But in a self-hosted environment it's harder to know how far behind an installation could be, so if we change the notification modelling it seems like this could lead to a situation where a freshly-pulled Docker image won't boot without human intervention.

Maybe that's overly cautious, but worth bearing in mind.

However I think we could write the migration in SQL. Might have to use correlated subqueries for the updates that require joins but it should still be faster than multiple queries. And populating the stacks could use an `insert ... select`.

Or we could define models inline. But the SQL approach should be considerably faster to run.

I wasn't sure of the context for this change, so main question is: currently we get grouped stacks in the tray, but we can click through to see the full history of the notifications in the index view. With this change, do we still have a way to view that full history? Or is the intention that we only every interact with stacks now?

Or in other words, the notifications list is now actually a list of the latest notification per card?

I couldn't think of a way for this not to be a breaking change in the API unless we continue to support both: a notification feed, and a notification stack feed. But I think whether we'd do that would depend on the motivation for this change, and what we want notifications to be. If they are always shown grouped, do we even need to store them at two levels? Could we keep only the stack level one, and update it when new card events happen?

body:
> The unread count is just the number of unread notifications in the stack, or in other words. the number of events for a card that you haven't seen.

That's why I'm wondering about the modelling here. We have events that happen to the card, and we (now) have a "notification stack", which is effectively the user-specific notification about the most recent even on that card. (Or as suggested in the Fizzy convo, maybe it's not exactly "most recent" if we also prioritize events where you were mentioned over those that happen later).

So if all the change information is in the event, and we track the read/unread state on the stack, what do we gain from persisting all those individual notifications as well? Could the events populate the notification stacks directly?

And if so, maybe this has a smaller impact on the API, if instead of introducing a new model we might be able to change the semantics of notifications a bit so that notifications de-dupe themselves appropriately. Might be simpler, and saves having a high-traffic table for something we aren't actually showing.

Also, if we are summarizing per card everywhere else, should we also do it in the email?

author: shetty-tejas
body:
While the implementation makes sense, I feel this might not be the right place for these changes. Here is why:

1. Using the `role=listbox` query will add this reordering behaviour to all multi-selection comboboxes, whether you want it or not. You won't have any way to control this behaviour. Ideally, this should be handled using a target.
2. This behaviour could be moved to a different controller. The current controller manages the core combobox implementation and is working fine. Since reordering is a cosmetic change, we can use an additional controller (preferably one that inherits multi_selection_combobox) for it. This way, the concerns remain well-segregated and the code stays decoupled.

author: rosa
body:
I was going to ask whether this was correct because it seemed strange to have a `particulars` key inside the `particulars` hash, but I see this is unfortunately the case in some of the event tracking calls. In some cases, the calls to `track_event` include an extra `particulars` key. This is the case in: 

```ruby
def track_board_change_event(old_board_name)
  track_event "board_changed", particulars: { old_board: old_board_name, new_board: board.name }
end

def track_title_change
  if title_before_last_save.present?
    track_event "title_changed", particulars: { old_title: title_before_last_save, new_title: title }
  end
end

track_event "triaged", particulars: { column: column.name }
```

And I see these are precisely the ones you're using here, which is unfortunate 😅 Ideally we'd fix the extra `particulars` key there, but that's out of scope for this change. 

Perhaps, to remove a bit of the repetition here, I'd add an extra method like this: 

```ruby
def event_particulars
  event.particulars.dig("particulars") || {}
end
``` 

And then use it like 
```ruby 
def  column_name
  event_particulars["column"]
end
```

author: djmb
body:
A few thoughts:

This won't work with MySQL because by default it requires tokens to be 3 characters or more. We should check that it doesn't break anything though.

We are now going to double stem data, once with mittens in Ruby and then a second time with the porter stemmer in the FTS5 SQLite implementation. This maybe works fine, but it seems a bit iffy, for example if the two stemming algorithms do not work the same way.

Ideally we should change the table to `tokenize='unicode61'` to avoid the SQLite tokenization.

I think we also will need to do a full reindex in a migration so the correctly stemmed data is stored.

Finally we should add some tests with CJK data to `searches_controller_test.rb` for a more complete testing. The setup is quite slow for those tests because they are not transactional so we might want a single test that tests a bunch of different queries.

author: jzimdars
body:
We had something like this at one point but there are a number of ways it can go wrong:

1. It's easier to refer to the "Fizzy menu" in documentation and conversation (and in support tickets) when it always is the same for everyone. Otherwise you have to say "Look for your account name at the top" and account name is not a huge part of this app. 
2. We'd have to figure out a new default name for accounts. I believe when you create a second Fizzy account it's named automatically something like "Jason's Fizzy" or "Jason't 2nd Fizzy" and so you'd have "Jason's Fizzy Fizzy" in the menu. 
3. Obviously if the account name is too long or too many words and we have to truncate.
4. Some words or phrases followed by "Fizzy" could be awkward.
5. This could be a pro or con, but most people just won't have multiple accounts so you could argue that this isn't worth the change or that it doesn't matter because it won't affect many users.

My preference is to stick with the current design which makes it clear how to know which account you're in and easy to switch without putting it into the most important element on the screen all the time. Appreciate the idea, @newstler!

Updated in 973ff66:

- **FTS5 `tokenize='unicode61'`** — this avoids the double-stemming (Mittens + porter). Added a migration that recreates the table and reindexes.

author: monorkin
body:
I moved the Passkey / Credential model down to ActionPack - similar to ActiveStorage::Blob is in ActiveStorage. I think this model will be fairly static, but if someone needs to add something they can do so with a mixin. I added out name auto-suggestion and icon as a mixin to test it out.

I also moved decoding and validation further down the call chain.

And to simplify the public interface I added a `Holder` mixin that adds `has_passkeys`. People can then configure passkey registration and authentication params through that method.

```ruby
class Identity < ApplicationRecord
  include ActionPack::WebAuthn::Holder

  has_passkeys do |config|
    config.creation_options do
      {
        name: email_address,
        display_name: Current.user&.name || email_address
      }
    end
  end

  # ...
```

There is now also a configuration option to set default registration or authentication methods too.

I'm thinking of returning to the Credential naming, now that the model is in ActionPack, as it covers both Passkeys and regular WebAuthn.

body:
@kevinmcconnell @dhh I implemented your suggestions

First, `has_passkeys` now accepts options with which you can configure both request and creation options:
```ruby
has_passkeys name: :full_name, display_name: :email_address
```
I kept the block configuration for now, let me know if you think it's better to remove it. 
It offers no advantage over the options hash, I find it to be a nice way to configure things, but if it will be unused then better to remove it.

I also renamed ActionPack::WebAuthn::Passkey to ActionPack::Passkey and put Holder and the form helpers under that namespace.

Second, I added a `create_passkey_button`, `sign_in_with_passkey_button`, `passkey_request_options_meta_tag` and `passkey_creation_options_meta_tag` helpers together with JS to make them work and switched Fizzy over to use them. In the end I didn't need any functions exposed on window, and the conditional mediation logic that we use in Fizzy is now all handled by ActionPack.

Lastly, I updated the examples in the PR description to reflect all the changes.

Thanks for tracking this down.

I'm wondering if the blob filtering could be simpler. The `internal_only_blob_ids` / `external_blob_ids` logic seems to be protecting against a blob that's attached to both an `Export` and a real account record simultaneously. But looking at `ZipFile`, every export always creates a fresh blob — so that shared-blob scenario shouldn't be possible in practice.

If that's right, would this be sufficient for both `BlobRecordSet` and `FileRecordSet`?

```ruby
def records
  excluded_blob_ids = ::ActiveStorage::Attachment
    .where(account: account, record_type: %w[Export Account::Import])
    .select(:blob_id)

  ::ActiveStorage::Blob.where(account: account).where.not(id: excluded_blob_ids)
end
```

Am I missing a case where a blob could legitimately be shared between an export and a real record?

(`AttachmentRecordSet` looks right to me as-is.)

When it encounters an `ActiveStorage::Attachment` with `record_type: "Export"` or `"Account::Import"`, it calls `verify_model_type` which raises `IntegrityError: "Unrecognized model type"` because those types aren’t in the whitelist. Altough the file is uploaded (I tried both local and S3) the data is never added to fizzy.

Then I noitced the doubling of the size becuase I thought the problem was with the export, so I kept asking for one and each time the import failed, I’d re-export to get a fresh file. I noticed the export ZIP kept roughly doubling in size.

You’re right... the shared-blob scenario can’t happen in practice. Both the S3 path `create_before_direct_upload!` and the disk path `attachment.attach(io: tempfile, ...)` in `ZipFile.create_for` always create a fresh blob. author: flavorjones
body: The connection pool delegation in `active_storage.rb` is the fix. Previously, `ActiveStorage::Record` and `ApplicationRecord` had separate connection pools, which meant `belongs_to :record, touch: true` on `ActiveStorage::Attachment` silently failed — the card could not join the attachment's transaction. Sharing the pool makes the existing `touch: true` mechanism work correctly, so no explicit `record.touch` is needed.

body: Good catch. Restored the `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block as a no-JS fallback with a `:not([data-motion="animate"])` guard so the JS-driven "Always animate" mode still overrides it. Fixed in c2130d8d7.

author: xseman
body: The patch is specifically required for Turbo. Its `prefersViewTransitions` getter hardcodes `!window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches` and completely ignores `data-motion`. Without the patch, "Always animate" has no effect on view transitions when the OS has `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` set. The patch is intentionally scoped to `prefers-reduced-motion` queries and reads `dataset.motion` dynamically, so it only intercepts the one check we need to override.

Marcel is a **transitive dependency** in fizzy, pulled in via ActiveStorage (`marcel (~> 1.0)`). Fizzy has **no direct references** to `Marcel::` (confirmed: only `Gemfile.lock` mentions it). It is exercised indirectly: ActiveStorage calls `Marcel::MimeType.for(io, name:, declared_type:)`, `Marcel::Magic.new`, `Marcel::Magic.child?`, and `Marcel::Magic.by_extension` when identifying/serving attachments.

**Public API is unchanged** across this range. author: vitalibondar
body:
Thanks for the automated review! Quick notes on the three comments:

**`app/models/search/query.rb:36` and `app/models/search/stemmer.rb:8` — `[[:word:]]` is intentional and correct.** In Ruby (Onigmo), the inner `[...]` is a *nested* character class, not a literal `[`. So `/[^[[:word:]]"]/` means "anything that is not a word character and not a quote" — there is no stray literal `[` admitted to the set. Verified:

```ruby
"a[b фільтр".gsub(/[^[[:word:]]"]/, " ")  # => "a b фільтр"  (the "[" is stripped)
"a[b фільтр".gsub(/[^\p{Word}"]/,   " ")  # => "a b фільтр"  (identical)
```

`/[^[[:word:]]"]/` and `/[^\p{Word}"]/` produce byte-identical output across the inputs I tried (Cyrillic, brackets, quotes, hyphenated). Happy to switch to `\p{Word}` if you prefer it for readability — no behavioural difference.

**`test/models/search_test.rb` — assertion style.** I mirrored the existing `assert results.find { |it| it.card_id == card.id }` pattern used by the neighbouring tests in this file for consistency. Glad to switch to `any?`/`card_id` inclusion if that is the preference.

body: Good catch on the direction — we adopted the row lock. Worth clarifying the mechanism though: the DB increment itself is atomic (`increment!` compiles to `UPDATE accounts SET cards_count = cards_count + 1`), so increments are never lost at the counter level. The collision came from the stale in-memory *return* value — two requests both reading `cards_count = 100` and each computing `101`. We now wrap the increment in `account.with_lock` (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the account row) to serialize numbering per account, so the second request reads the already-incremented value. Retries removed entirely.

🤖 **Beta hit a second Action Cable edge break — fixed in 777e6f8.**

`NoMethodError: undefined method 'mutex' for nil` on every WebSocket connect (`ApplicationCable::Connection#connect`). Rails edge dropped `@server` from `ActionCable::SubscriptionAdapter::Base` (rails/rails `96b3add356`, *"Extract async executor from Action Cable event_loop"*, 2026-05-28 — same refactor cluster as the Sentry break) in favor of `@executor`/`@config`. Released `solid_cable` (incl. 4.0.0) still calls `@server.mutex`/`@server.event_loop`, so `@server` is nil at edge. `solid_cable` **main** adapts to both contracts, so this tracks `github: "rails/solid_cable"` until a fixed release ships.

**Why the suite didn't catch it (same blind spot as the Sentry fix):** `config/cable.yml` uses `adapter: test` in the test env; beta/staging use `adapter: solid_cable`. Tests never exercise the real adapter. Verified by reproducing the exact failing path (instantiate the SolidCable adapter → `subscribe`) before/after the bump; OSS (1510) + SaaS (1626) unit suites green.

author: Maklu
body:
@AndreasNasman Yes, this fixes that too. On main, query sanitization strips any non-ASCII letter before the search runs (Ruby's `\w` is ASCII-only), so "hälsa" becomes "h lsa" — same root cause as the CJK breakage. This PR switches the sanitizer to Unicode-aware character classes (`\p{L}\p{N}`), which fixes accented Latin characters as well. I've added a test with Swedish content (runs on both SQLite and MySQL) to keep it covered.

One limitation: stemming is English-only, so inflected forms won't match each other (e.g. "hälsa" vs "hälsan"), but exact word matches work.

author: Maklu
body: Fixed in 1dbb5eb3e with the sentinel approach — matches are wrapped in private-use characters (U+E000/U+E001) during the term passes, and the real markup is swapped in only after all terms are processed. Added tests covering query terms that collide with the markup ("test class", "some text").

author: Maklu
body: These two regexes accept exactly the same set of match start positions: the trailing `[a-zA-Z0-9_]*(?![a-zA-Z0-9_])` in `highlight` is always satisfiable (the greedy run extends to the end of the ASCII word, at which point the lookahead holds), so it only affects match length, not whether or where a match starts. The lookbehind and the term are identical in both, so a snippet is always centered on a position `highlight` also marks.

author: Maklu
body: Added `\p{M}` in 1dbb5eb3e, together with the stemmer tokenizer so both sides stay consistent. This matters beyond NFD Latin, too — combining marks are integral to scripts like Devanagari or Thai, where stripping them shattered words into single consonants.

author: Maklu
body: Done in 1dbb5eb3e, together with the sanitizer change above. Added tests for NFD input and Devanagari, plus an end-to-end test that a decomposed-form query still matches (runs on both SQLite and MySQL).

author: Maklu
body: Right — the single-character tokens fall under MySQL's default `innodb_ft_min_token_size` (3), so CJK stays unindexed on MySQL. It's not a regression though: on main, CJK queries never reach `MATCH` at all — the sanitizer strips CJK characters to whitespace — so CJK search doesn't work on MySQL either way, and longer contiguous runs being indexable there doesn't help for the same reason. Proper MySQL support means the ngram fulltext parser plus rebuilding the fulltext indexes on existing installations, which I'd rather keep as a follow-up than fold into this PR. Latin/accented tokens keep their full length, so MySQL behavior for those is unchanged (the accented-characters test runs on both adapters). Added a known-limitation section to the PR description.

author: Maklu
body: Scoped it explicitly now — the PR description has a known-limitation section: CJK search is fully supported on SQLite, and on MySQL it remains unavailable exactly as on main, where the sanitizer strips CJK from queries before they run. MySQL support via the ngram parser is a follow-up since it requires rebuilding fulltext indexes on existing installations.

author: jeremy

🤖 Broadened to fix the whole defect class in one PR (per our fix-comprehensively practice — the diagnosis found three instances of the same idiom).

**Second commit** applies the identical fix to two more controllers that use the same broken `removeEventListener(fn.bind(this))` idiom:
- `tooltip_controller.js` (`mouseenter`/`mouseout`)
- `dialog_manager_controller.js` (`dialog:show`)

These bind to `this.element` rather than `document`, so they **don't** leak unbounded like the drag_and_strum one (the listener dies when the element is GC'd) — but they stack duplicate listeners across a disconnect/reconnect of the same element (cached Turbo previews, morphing), firing the handler N times per event. The `document`-scoped `drag_and_strum` leak (first commit) is the one that causes the reported Safari/PWA freeze; these two are same-pattern hygiene.

Captured as a reusable pattern (`event-listener-removal-identity-mismatch`) so `/coworker-hunt` can sweep other apps.

body: Keeping this deliberately — the observation is accurate, but a full `-Syu` is the only supported way to converge a repo-owned mise on Arch: the same pacman doctrine this PR's packages phase now honors (no `-Sy` + targeted `-S`) forbids upgrading mise in isolation, and `pacman -Sy mise` / `-S mise` against a stale DB are exactly the partial-upgrade shapes to avoid. Context bounds the blast radius: our pacman machines are Omarchy fleet boxes that already converge via full `pacman -Syu` on every Shipyard run, this branch only fires when a pacman-owned mise is below the 2026.7.5 floor (one-time per floor bump), and the alternative — stopping with "run sudo pacman -Syu yourself" — adds a manual step to reach the identical end state. If setup-driven full upgrades prove surprising in the fresh pacman matrix, the cheap reversal is swapping this branch for that guided stop.

author: jeremy
body:
🤖 Closing in deference to #2988 (`security/ssrf-ipv6-transition-guard`), which lands a more complete IPv6 SSRF guard: it extracts the embedded IPv4 from a NAT64 address and re-checks it (so NAT64→public still resolves while NAT64→internal is blocked), blocks 6to4/Teredo outright, and adds comprehensive IPv4/IPv6 special-use ranges. That supersedes this range-blocklist approach. Thanks @djmb.

One gap to carry over — noted on #2988 directly: the well-known-prefix check keys only on `64:ff9b::/96`, so the RFC 8215 local-use NAT64 prefix `64:ff9b:1::/48` (e.g. `64:ff9b:1::a00:1` → `10.0.0.1`) still reads as public.

author: jeremy
body:
🤖 One gap worth closing while you're in here: `NAT64_WELL_KNOWN` keys only on `64:ff9b::/96` (RFC 6052). RFC 8215 also defines a **local-use** NAT64 prefix, `64:ff9b:1::/48`, which embeds IPv4 the same way. So `64:ff9b:1::a00:1` decodes to `10.0.0.1` but falls through the WKP check into `disallowed_ipv6?`, where it reads as a public IPv6 address and is allowed — the embedded IPv4 never gets re-checked.

Suggest extending the well-known-prefix match (or the `embedded_ipv4` recheck) to cover `64:ff9b:1::/48` as well. The low 32 bits carry the IPv4 in both prefixes, so the same `embedded_ipv4(ipaddr)` extraction works for local-use once the prefix guard admits it.

Repro address: `64:ff9b:1::a00:1` → `10.0.0.1` (should block); `64:ff9b:1::808:808` → `8.8.8.8` (should still resolve).

author: djmb
body:
Fixed in 95b2d43ed. `NAT64_WELL_KNOWN` is now `NAT64_PREFIXES`, covering both the well-known prefix and the RFC 8215 local-use prefix `64:ff9b:1::/48`, with the same embedded-IPv4 recheck — `64:ff9b:1::a00:1` (→ 10.0.0.1) blocks, `64:ff9b:1::808:808` (→ 8.8.8.8) still resolves. Both cases have regression tests.

Also added `2001:2::/48` (IPv6 benchmarking, RFC 5180) to `DISALLOWED_IPV6_RANGES` to match the IPv4 `198.18.0.0/15` block — the same gap Copilot caught on the once-campfire counterpart (basecamp/once-campfire#225).
